title: Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
summary:
Yup, sounds very familiar :) Claude code + API access to LLMs can suck you in. Hoping a saner workflow emerges down the line.
Quoting @nasqret
I've just finished a week where I have been using agentic workflows basically 24/7. Here are some impressions:
1. I am extremely tired. Supervision of so many projects is distracting, frustrating and exhausting.
2. I have never worked on so many fronts at once. It's not only a superficial impression. I've read a ton, did courses with students, coded, learned new mathematical theorems, explored new git repos.
3. The more you work with agents, the better you become at instructing them. Don't overthink the prompts. Doing things step by step and letting the agent guide you is very productive.
4. I failed in some of those
projects. Basically I got the impression that I could do everything with the agent. Maybe, but time
and tokens are constrained.
5. I don't use much ready made software anymore. I build or scaffold stuff that I need. My favorite modality is text and best interface is simple text API. Everything can be pipelined.
6. Mathematics can be treated as software. Whatever you need to do with it, it can be decomposed into small
parts. The thinking bit is still mostly done in my brain if necessary.
7. I think of my past life as a warm-up for this new period. The offline reading, coding and internalizing was super important. Without it, I would be a pure vibe-coder. With training, you sail a ship.
8. I don't want to see my paychecks. It's expensive, because the better you get, the more you spend on more and more projects. You abandon them in a more advanced state, but there is a token price to pay.
9. Each time I see a challenge, I think whether I can find a solution with the agent. I don't skip tasks. Sometimes I feel overly optimistic. It's part of the learning to see where the agents are limited.
10. I think I master entirely new workflows. They are not properly described in the books. It's a
brave new world. Each standard task
can be turned into a task for the agent. It's very enabling.
Happy coding everyone!

title: Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
summary:
Excellent point: while some experts will refuse to change their old workflows, many will embrace these new tools and try to open interesting new avenues. Currently they might be spending years getting to understand a new area, and that may speed up with an AI assistant.
Quoting @IAmTimNguyen
Mathematics as a field is going to have to reorient itself in light of powerful AI. But a slight pushback to Gowers's comment:
"If LLMs are at the point where they can solve 'gentle problems', ...the lower bound for contributing to mathematics will now be to prove something that LLMs can’t prove, rather than simply to prove something that nobody has proved up to now and that at least somebody finds interesting."
Mathematics is infinite and thus inexhaustible. By having powerful AIs that can do heavy lifting, more of the burden is shifted towards taste and asking the right question. The possibility of discovering something by looking in the right place that everyone else missed becomes possible. In mathematical physics for instance, an Einstein with inspiration of the equivalence principle might not have to toil for a decade to invent general relativity, but could have equations proposed, their solutions found, and scenarios validated as limits of Newtonian physics. Contributing to mathematics, rather than having the bar raised for problem-solving, has opened up for ideation and generation.

title: Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
summary:
Probably (let me say almost certainly) wrong if the main finding is in Table 1. Max thinking budget = 10K tokens. Hence comfortably within capabilities of a single call. Multi-agent reasoning helps when you need to generate say 1M tokens. Possible in a single call but ineffective.
Quoting @rohanpaul_ai
New Stanford paper argues that, under equal reasoning budgets, one LLM usually solves multi-hop problems better than many coordinated ones.
The core point is almost embarrassingly simple.
A single agent keeps the whole problem in one internal chain of thought, while a multi-agent system has to slice that chain into messages, summaries, and handoffs.
Every handoff is a compression step.
And once reasoning is compressed, some information is easier to drop than to recover, which is why the paper leans on the Data Processing Inequality as a formal explanation rather than just an empirical hunch.
The experiments back that up across Qwen, DeepSeek, and Gemini on FRAMES and MuSiQue: when thinking-token budgets are matched, single-agent systems usually match or beat sequential, debate, role-based, and ensemble setups.
Here’s the part most people miss.
Many celebrated multi-agent gains may not be architectural gains at all. They often come from spending more test-time compute, surfacing more visible reasoning, or benefiting from evaluation quirks that make the pipeline look smarter than it is.
The paper is especially sharp when it looks for the boundary case instead of pretending the rule is universal.
When the single agent’s effective context is degraded by masking, substitution, or misleading distractors, multi-agent pipelines become more competitive and sometimes win, not because message passing is magical, but because structure can partially stabilize corrupted reasoning.
That is a much narrower and more useful claim than “more agents is better.”
It suggests the real trade-off is not single versus multi so much as latent reasoning versus external coordination, with context quality and compute accounting deciding which side looks stronger.
For multi-hop reasoning, the default should now be clear: start with one strong model, and treat extra agents as a repair strategy, not an upgrade.
----
Paper Link – arxiv. org/abs/2604.02460
Paper Title: "Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets"

clean_title: Self-Distillation Zero: Turning Binary Rewards into Dense Supervision with Self-Revision
summary:
SD-Zero is selected for an oral presentation at the ICML RLxF workshop! See you in Korea 🥳
💻Check out our code:
Quoting @yinghui_he_
RLVR gives sparse supervision; On-Policy Self-Distillation often requires high-quality demonstrations. Our new method, ✨SD-Zero✨, gets the best of both worlds – we use model’s self-revision to turn binary rewards into dense token-level supervision. No external teacher. No curated demonstrations.
🚨 Introducing Self-Distillation Zero (SD-Zero), which trains one model to play two roles: (1) “Generator” that makes attempts, and (2) “Reviser” that conditions on the generator’s failed/successful attempt + binary reward to produce a better answer. ‼️Even WRONG attempts can become the training signal.‼️
🔗Paper:
🏆 SD-Zero brings 10%+ improvement over base models (Qwen3,4B; Olmo3,7B) on math & code reasoning, beating GRPO and vanilla On-Policy Self-Distillation under the same training budget. SD-Zero also enables iterative self-evolution.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGFMrufWsAAwNvb.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGFMrufXAAAMydB.png
clean_summary:
SD-Zero is a new method selected for an oral presentation at the ICML RLxF workshop. It trains a single model to both generate attempts and revise them using its own self-revision process, transforming binary rewards into dense token-level supervision without needing external teachers or curated demonstrations.

SD-Zero achieves over 10% improvement on math and code reasoning tasks for models like Qwen3 and Olmo, outperforming previous methods such as GRPO and vanilla On-Policy Self-Distillation under the same training budget. It also enables iterative self-evolution, making models better through self-guided improvement.

🚀 New paper: Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs
👉 LLMs often fail not because the answer is impossible, but because they miss the one decisive clue hidden in a long trace or image.
🔥 We introduce ContextRL: RL that teaches models to identify which context actually supports an answer.
✅ +2.2% on 5 agentic benchmarks
✅ +1.8% across 12 VQA benchmarks
✅ Works for coding agents & multimodal reasoning
✅ Same contrastive data, but better objective — not data augmentation
🧠 The key idea: don’t only reward the final answer. Reward the model for grounding it in the right evidence.
📄 Paper:

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLBw5MbaAAAT8Rb.jpg
clean_summary:
A new paper introduces ContextRL, a reinforcement learning approach that trains language models to identify which parts of a long trace or image actually support an answer. This method improves performance by rewarding models for grounding their answers in the right evidence, rather than just the final result.

The results show a 2.2% improvement on five agentic benchmarks and a 1.8% boost across 12 visual question answering benchmarks. The approach works for coding agents and multimodal reasoning, using the same contrastive data but with a better objective instead of data augmentation. The key idea is to reward models for grounding their answers in the right evidence, leading to better reasoning and accuracy.

title: Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
clean_title: Surprising findings on AI safety and the role of thinking tokens in small models
summary:
Surprising finding about AI safety from our group. We find that in small open-parameter models, the thinking tokens have almost no effect on safety. On unsafe prompts, the refusal/compliance is predictable from a simple trained head given the prompt alone. Great work and thread by @narutatsuri
Quoting @narutatsuri
New Paper: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
Reasoning models generate “thinking” tokens before answering, which improves performance on many tasks like math and coding.
A natural hope is that models can also use thinking to deliberate about whether to refuse or comply a request.
But how true is this?
We find a surprisingly sobering answer: current reasoning models often do not use thinking tokens for real safety deliberation.
Work with: Abhishek Panigrahi, @prfsanjeevarora at @PrincetonPLI
(More in 🧵below)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMoy4U3aQAALxvx.png
clean_summary: Sanjeev Arora reports a surprising discovery about AI safety in small open-parameter models. The study finds that thinking tokens have almost no effect on safety, and on unsafe prompts, the model's refusal or compliance can be predicted from a simple trained head given the prompt alone. This suggests that current reasoning models often do not use thinking tokens for genuine safety deliberation, highlighting a limitation in how models handle safety considerations.

title: Sanjeev Arora (@prfsanjeevarora)
clean_title: Self-Distill-Zero: Self-Improvement for Instruct Models Using Self-Distillation
summary:
Self-Distill-Zero is a very simple self-improvement pipeline for instruct models in settings with a reward/correctness judge. Model M given question q trains via online distillation loss using as teacher M with input (q, a, s) where a= answer generated by M and s=judge's numeric score for a. This self-distillation in effect lets M to provide dense token-level supervision to itself. On math and coding it handily outperforms SFT and RL baselines. Kudos to the student team and 1st author @yinghui_he_
Quoting @yinghui_he_
SD-Zero was selected as the 🏆 Best Paper at the ICML RLxF workshop, and 🏆 Honorable Mention at AI4Math workshop! 🍻
👉Please check out our oral presentation tomorrow (7/10) at 9:10-10:00 AM, Grand Ballroom 101-102!
Also presenting another Best Paper at RLxF led by the amazing @_yongjinny: "Transferability for General Reasoning: An Automated Curriculum for Multi-Domain RLVR" 🥳
🔗Paper links:
SD-Zero:
TAC:
clean_summary: Self-Distill-Zero is a straightforward self-improvement pipeline for instruct models that operate with a reward or correctness judge. It involves training the model via online distillation loss, where the model teaches itself by using its own generated answers and the judge's scores as dense token-level supervision. This method significantly outperforms supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) baselines on math and coding tasks. The approach has been recognized with awards at ICML and AI4Math workshops, highlighting its effectiveness in turning binary rewards into dense supervision for model improvement.
